attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack post, published under his name. He is not quoting anyone else.

semantics.note: Matches the source clause and keeps 'thus far'. It correctly avoids narrowing the claim to AI. The 'If... any sign' opener is rhetorical framing, not a real condition on the legislature clause. This is a firm retrospective observation.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary and fair: Congress had imposed little meaningful restriction on the tech industry by June 5, 2024, with narrow exceptions allowed by 'almost no'. The result depends on how much weight narrow enacted laws get against the lack of broad reform, which the speaker did not specify.

evidence.note: May 15, 2024 reporting: no major AI-regulation law had passed Congress, and the Senate roadmap was preliminary. Covers the AI part of tech regulation only.
May 31, 2024 CRS report: the comprehensive privacy bill (APRA) was still a draft at subcommittee stage. So the major privacy effort was still only a proposal.

COPPA (1998) puts real duties on online operators that collect children's data. It is a narrow, long-standing law, so it is only a weak counterpoint and fits the limited exceptions that 'almost no' allows.

The INFORM Act (enacted Dec 2022) imposes seller-verification and disclosure duties on online marketplaces, enforced by the FTC. A real enacted constraint, but narrow in scope. It weakens the claim without overturning it.

reviews.rationale: Under the contract's plain reading, the support condition is met. As of mid-2024, the major efforts on AI and comprehensive privacy were still proposals (e1, e2). The enacted constraints shown, COPPA and INFORM (e3, e4), are narrow, and 'almost no' allows limited exceptions. The packet is not a full inventory of tech legislation, but on this evidence the broad description holds.
